note: Supplements intel/counterevidence/energy_infra_counterevidence_result.json (which found COUNTEREVIDENCE_GAP on 4 directions against the 597-doc LOCAL corpus only). This file records live WebFetch/WebSearch results from this session, against the 10 directions requested for this pilot. Status is per-direction and honest; EVIDENCE_FOUND here means real content was fetched and read, not that it fully refutes H1.

1_DATA_CENTER_EFFICIENCY_IMPROVEMENTS.finding: Hyperscale PUE near theoretical limit (~1.1) yet Google total energy rose 3.7x 2016-2022 -- efficiency gains observed but NOT shown to offset aggregate growth; this is evidence of a Jevons-paradox dynamic, which argues AGAINST the simple 'efficiency will solve AI energy growth' counter-narrative, while still confirming real efficiency improvement occurred at the component level.

2_AI_HARDWARE_EFFICIENCY_GAINS.source: https://www.networkworld.com/article/3550686/as-global-ai-energy-usage-mounts-nvidia-claims-it-has-reduced-its-consumption-by-up-to-110000x.html (NVIDIA VP presentation at AI Summit DC, reported by Network World)
2_AI_HARDWARE_EFFICIENCY_GAINS.finding: NVIDIA claims ~100,000x energy-per-token reduction for inference and ~2,000x for training over roughly 10 years of GPU generations (2014-era hardware vs. Blackwell); article explicitly notes these are vendor-claimed figures with no independent third-party verification, and the 100,000x figure applies specifically to token-generation inference, not all AI workloads.
2_AI_HARDWARE_EFFICIENCY_GAINS.ai_attribution: DIRECT (AI-accelerator-specific) but evidence_strength is VENDOR_CLAIM, not independently measured -- recorded honestly as such, not upgraded to an independently-verified efficiency finding.

3_ELECTRICITY_DEMAND_GROWTH_PREDATES_AI_.note: IEA exec summary does show data center electricity growth at ~12%/yr 'since 2017', i.e. before ChatGPT-era AI boom (commonly dated ~2022-2023), which is PARTIAL support that the growth trend is not purely AI-originated, though IEA attributes recent acceleration specifically to AI. Flagged as PARTIAL EVIDENCE_FOUND, not fully run.

4_MANUFACTURING_RESHORING_DEMAND.source: Grid Strategies LLC, "Power Demand Forecasts Revised Up for Third Year Running, Led by Data Centers" (2025) and "Strategic Industries Surging: Driving US Power Demand" (2024), https://gridstrategiesllc.com/wp-content/uploads/Grid-Strategies-National-Load-Growth-Report-2025.pdf ; https://gridstrategiesllc.com/wp-content/uploads/National-Load-Growth-Report-2024.pdf
4_MANUFACTURING_RESHORING_DEMAND.finding: Grid Strategies' national load-growth reports name 'strategic industries' (semiconductor fabs, battery/EV manufacturing, hydrogen, LNG -- i.e. reshoring/industrial-policy-driven manufacturing) as an independently identified driver of rising utility load forecasts, alongside and distinct from data centers. Titles/report-level finding only was read in this pass (full report body not fetched); treat as EVIDENCE_FOUND at the level of 'a named, non-AI industrial driver exists in utility planning data', not as a quantified TWh split versus data-center/AI demand.
4_MANUFACTURING_RESHORING_DEMAND.ai_attribution: NONE (manufacturing/reshoring is explicitly a non-AI driver by construction)

5_EV_ELECTRIFICATION_DEMAND.finding: OBSERVED: global EV charging consumed ~180 TWh of electricity in 2024 (~0.7% of final global electricity consumption), a 60% increase over 2023. FORECAST (IEA Stated Policies Scenario): EV electricity demand could grow more than fourfold to ~780 TWh by 2030 (~2.5% of global electricity demand; >4% in Europe, 3.6% in China). No US-specific TWh figure was given in the fetched section. This is real, independent (non-AI) electricity-demand growth, confirming EV charging as a genuine alternative/parallel driver, though at roughly half the 2024 OBSERVED scale of data center consumption (180 TWh vs. 415 TWh) and not shown to explain data-center-specific grid bottlenecks (e.g. PJM).

6_POPULATION_GROWTH.finding: EIA attributes the recent reversal of a near-two-decade electricity-consumption plateau primarily to the COMMERCIAL sector (explicitly including data centers, forecast +2.6%/yr 2020-2026) and INDUSTRIAL sector (including manufacturing, +2.1%/yr), while the RESIDENTIAL sector -- the segment most directly tied to population growth -- is forecast to grow slowest (+0.7%/yr) and is described as driven by temperature, not population. This is real evidence AGAINST population growth as a primary driver of the current demand surge, and is consistent with (not a refutation of) the data-center/AI-adjacent attribution, while also naming industrial/manufacturing growth as a comparably-sized co-driver.
6_POPULATION_GROWTH.ai_attribution: NOT_APPLICABLE (counts against a non-AI alternative, not evidence about AI itself)

7_WEATHER_CLIMATE_DEMAND.source: EIA, "June heat wave increased electricity demand in the eastern and midwestern United States" https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=62410 ; EIA, "Texas power grid met record-breaking demand for electricity during recent heat wave" https://www.eia.gov/todayinEnergy/detail.php?id=57240 ; Ember, "Powering through the heat: how 2024 heatwaves reshaped electricity demand" https://ember-energy.org/latest-insights/powering-through-the-heat-how-2024-heatwaves-reshaped-electricity-demand/
7_WEATHER_CLIMATE_DEMAND.finding: Multiple independent EIA Today-in-Energy notes and an Ember analysis document that 2024/2025 heat waves drove record or near-record peak electricity demand in ERCOT (Texas) and the Eastern Interconnection, via air-conditioning load. This is a real, non-AI, weather-driven demand channel, operating on peak/hourly timescales rather than the annual TWh growth trend the AI_ENERGY_INFRA claims track -- so it is a genuine alternative explanation for PEAK LOAD STRESS episodes specifically, not for the multi-year baseline electricity-growth trend.
7_WEATHER_CLIMATE_DEMAND.ai_attribution: NONE (weather-driven peak demand is a non-AI driver by construction)

8_NON_AI_CLOUD_GROWTH.finding: Paper's dataset and argument are about general cloud computing (ads-funded free services etc.), not AI specifically -- supports that non-AI cloud growth is a real, independently documented driver, though the paper does not quantify it against AI's share.

9_GRID_INVESTMENT_ALREADY_PLANNED_PRE_AI.finding: GridLab documents ~130 GW of generation (largely renewables/battery) already in PJM's interconnection queue -- i.e., capacity additions in progress -- but does not establish these were planned independent of / prior to AI-driven demand growth; queue delays are attributed broadly to 'data center additions and electrification', not isolated from AI. Cannot be read as clean counterevidence without more sourcing.

10_REGIONS_WITH_DC_GROWTH_NO_REPORTED_PO.note: O-1 search surfaced industry/advocacy pieces arguing data-center load growth is 'not necessarily a problem' in general (e.g. ITIF, 'The United States Needs Data Centers, and Data Centers Need Energy, but That Is Not Necessarily a Problem', https://itif.org/publications/2025/11/24/united-states-needs-data-centers-data-centers-need-energy-but-that-is-not-necessarily-a-problem/) but no source was found that names a SPECIFIC region with substantial data-center growth and documents an absence of grid/price/interconnection stress there. Recorded as SEARCH_RUN_NO_CLEAR_EVIDENCE rather than EVIDENCE_FOUND -- this is an honest negative result, not a gap filled.

honest_conclusion: Across O-0 + O-1: of the original 10 requested directions, 7 now have real fetched/read evidence (efficiency improvements, non-AI cloud growth, AI hardware efficiency [vendor-claimed], EV electrification demand, population growth [evidence AGAINST], manufacturing/reshoring, weather/climate [peak-load timescale only]), 2 remain partially evidenced (pre-AI-boom growth trend, grid investment already planned), and 1 (region with DC growth and no power problems) was searched in O-1 and found no qualifying source -- an honest SEARCH_RUN_NO_CLEAR_EVIDENCE result, not fabricated and not left as SEARCH_NOT_RUN.
